screens.title: I2C and SPI: Connecting Multiple Devices Efficiently
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we explore two essential communication buses used with Arduino: I2C and SPI. You will learn what makes I2C efficient for sharing two wires across many devices using addresses, and why SPI is chosen when you need higher speed and lower latency. We will walk through Arduino pin assignments for both buses, look at common devices that use each protocol, and practice reading and writing with library examples. You will also see how to detect address conflicts on an I2C bus and how to wire multiple SPI devices using separate select lines. These skills matter because they let you expand a single microcontroller into a larger system of sensors, displays, and storage without running out of pins. By the end you will be able to pick the right bus, wire it reliably, and use simple Arduino code to communicate with peripherals. As you explore, notice trade-offs: pin count, speed, and device support. Think about a small project you might build and which protocol would fit it best.

Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › I2C and SPI Overview
I2C and SPI
Understand shared buses, wiring, Arduino pins, and practical trade-offs for sensors and displays.
In this lesson
Pin mapping, code examples, and a practical scanner for I2C address conflicts.
Why it matters
Choosing the right bus saves pins and avoids timing problems when adding many devices.
Explore Key Topics
I2C Wiring
SDA and SCL plus pull-ups; multiple devices share the bus by address.
SPI Signals
MOSI, MISO, SCK, and separate SS lines per device for selection.
Picking a Bus
Consider pin count, speed needs, and library support for your sensors.
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass
Concept map
I2C
SDA, SCL, addresses — great for many low-speed sensors.
SPI

Practical link

Quick start

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: These four objectives map to the practical skills you need for working with I2C and SPI. First, you'll explain the technical differences between the two buses and what each signal means. Understanding that difference helps you choose the right interface for a sensor or display. Second, you'll wire multiple I2C devices to the same bus and manage unique 7-bit addresses; we will practice finding addresses and resolving conflicts. Third, you'll identify the SPI signal names—MOSI, MISO, SCK, and SS—and wire multiple SPI devices, including how to use separate slave select lines. Finally, you'll make protocol choices for common parts by weighing pin count, speed, and library support. Each objective includes hands-on practice so you learn to reason about trade-offs instead of memorizing facts. By the end you should be able to explain your choice to a peer and sketch the wiring for a small multi-device project with confidence.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › Learning Objectives - Practice
Hands-on activity
Connect an I2C LCD and an I2C RTC to the same SDA/SCL bus and display time. Run a scanner to find addresses and resolve conflicts if they occur.
Why this helps
This activity teaches addressing, bus sharing, and basic library usage so you can combine multiple I2C parts safely.
Assessment idea
If you must connect three sensors and a display with few pins, prefer I2C and explain the choice based on two-wire sharing and 7-bit addresses.
Common pitfalls
  • Forgetting pull-ups on SDA and SCL, causing noisy or absent signals.
  • Using the same SS pin for multiple SPI devices and not toggling it correctly.
  • Assuming every device uses the same default I2C address — always scan first.

screens.title: I2C basics: two-wire bus and addressing
screens.narratorSegment: I2C is a bus designed to let many devices share the same two wires: one for data and one for the clock. The data line is called SDA and the clock is SCL. Each device on the bus has a 7-bit address used by the master to initiate communication and target a peripheral. This means you can wire multiple sensors and small displays to the same two pins as long as no two devices use the same address. A typical Arduino Uno maps SDA to analog pin A4 and SCL to A5, although newer boards expose dedicated SDA and SCL pins. A concrete example is an I2C LCD and an I2C temperature sensor both connected to SDA and SCL; the master writes a display update to the LCD address and polls the sensor address for readings. A common misconception is that I2C requires no pull-ups: in fact both SDA and SCL are open-drain and need pull-up resistors on the bus to create valid logic highs. The key takeaway is that I2C trades speed for a minimal wiring footprint; use it when pin economy is more important than maximum throughput. How would you check addresses before wiring a second device?

keyIdea.title: I2C definition
keyIdea.text: Two shared wires with unique 7-bit addresses let many devices coexist; pull-ups are required for reliable signaling.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › I2C basics
Definition
I2C uses SDA (data) and SCL (clock). Devices use 7-bit addresses so multiple peripherals share the bus.
Signals
SDA: bidirectional data. SCL: clock generated by the master.
Key takeaway
Open-drain lines need pull-up resistors to form valid highs.
Common mistake
Wiring without checking device addresses leads to conflicts and silent devices.
Example scenario
An I2C LCD at address 0x27 and a temperature sensor at 0x48 both connect to SDA and SCL on the Uno. The master addresses each device by its 7-bit address to fetch readings or update the display.
Check your understanding
  • Why are pull-ups required for I2C?
  • How does a master address a single device on a shared bus?

screens.title: Wiring multiple I2C devices and avoiding address conflicts
screens.narratorSegment: Wiring multiple I2C devices follows a simple process but with a few checks to keep the bus healthy. First, connect all device SDA pins together and all SCL pins together, and connect those two lines to the Arduino SDA and SCL pins — on an Uno that is usually analog A4 and A5. Second, ensure appropriate pull-up resistors are present on SDA and SCL; some breakout boards include them, otherwise add 4.7 kilo-ohm resistors to 5 volts. Third, power each device and run an I2C scanner sketch to list active 7-bit addresses. The scanner identifies addresses so you can check for collisions. Fourth, if two devices share the same address, resolve it by changing the device address if possible, using an address translator, or moving to SPI for one of the parts. A concrete example: if a DS3231 clock and an OLED both show the same default address, run the scanner, then change the OLED's address via its configuration or use a software I2C multiplexer. A common misconception is that devices auto-negotiate addresses; they do not. The key takeaway is to always scan first and verify pull-ups; that prevents hours of debugging.

keyIdea.title: Wiring checklist
keyIdea.text: SDA together, SCL together, pull-ups enabled, run scanner, and resolve duplicate addresses before adding logic to your sketch.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › Wiring I2C Devices
Step-by-step
1. Tie all SDA lines together and to Arduino SDA (A4 on Uno). Tie all SCL lines together and to Arduino SCL (A5 on Uno).
2. Ensure pull-ups on SDA and SCL, typically 4.7 kilo-ohm to 5 V or 3.3 V depending on devices.
3. Power devices and run an I2C scanner sketch to list 7-bit addresses present on the bus.
4. If two devices share an address, change configuration, use a multiplexer, or choose SPI for one device.
Example
You wire an I2C LCD and a DS3231 RTC. After powering, the scanner shows addresses 0x27 and 0x68. The display updates and the clock responds because addresses are distinct and pull-ups are present.
Misconception
Devices do not share or change addresses automatically; the designer must check and manage addresses.

screens.title: Using the Wire library and an I2C LCD example
screens.narratorSegment: When programming I2C devices on Arduino, libraries encapsulate the low-level addressing and data framing so you work with objects instead of toggling pins. The Wire library provides the I2C primitives and many device libraries build on it. A common pattern is to create an object with the device address and call methods to send data. For example, a LiquidCrystal I2C library often uses a constructor that takes an address and display dimensions. In code you include the Wire header, include the device library, and instantiate the display object with its hex address and size. Conceptually, this object hides repeated start conditions, address bytes, and byte-level writes so you call familiar methods to print text. A concrete example: creating a display object at address 0x27 for a 16-by-2 LCD lets you call a method to set the cursor and print the time. A trap to avoid is assuming the default address for all modules — always scan to find the actual address. The takeaway is that library objects make code more readable and reduce mistakes, but you must still wire correctly and confirm addresses before relying on default constructors.

keyIdea.text: Device libraries wrap Wire functions into objects; instantiate with the device address and use high-level calls to update hardware.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › Wire & LiquidCrystal_I2C
Key code
#include <Wire.h>
#include <LiquidCrystal_I2C.h>
LiquidCrystal_I2C lcd(0x27, 16, 2);
This constructor creates a display object at address 0x27 with 16 columns and 2 rows. The library uses Wire behind the scenes to send bytes.
Example workflow
Initialize the display in setup, then use a print method inside loop to update text from a sensor or RTC. Libraries simplify cursor management and buffering.
Pro tip
Run the I2C scanner before relying on an address found in examples; many breakouts use different defaults.

screens.title: I2C scanner sketch and interpreting output
screens.narratorSegment: An I2C scanner sketch is the first diagnostic you should run on a new bus. It probes all possible 7-bit addresses and reports which ones respond. Running the scanner requires only the Wire library and a simple loop that attempts to begin transmission to each address; a responding device makes the library return success and you print the address. A concrete example output might list addresses like 0x27 and 0x68. Seeing two identical addresses indicates a conflict: two devices claim the same address and will not cooperate. The correct response is to check documentation for address selection options, change hardware configuration jumpers, use a multiplexer device, or move one peripheral to SPI if possible. A common misconception is that the scanner will test advanced features; it only reports that a device responded at that address. Use the scanner as an early check before writing higher-level code. The takeaway is simple: scanning saves time by confirming which devices are visible and where conflicts may exist. I2C scanner sketch and interpreting output means an i2c scanner confirms which 7-bit addresses respond and reveals collisions so you can fix wiring or configuration before coding.. In practical terms, detect addresses and resolve conflicts before integrating devices. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: An I2C scanner confirms which 7-bit addresses respond and reveals collisions so you can fix wiring or configuration before coding.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › I2C Scanner
What the scanner does
It probes each possible 7-bit address and prints the addresses that respond. Example output commonly shows hex addresses like 0x27 and 0x68.
Interpreter note
The scanner reports presence only; it does not identify device type. Use documentation to map address to part.
Conflict resolution
  • Check if the device allows changing its address via solder pads or jumpers.
  • Use an I2C multiplexer to isolate identical-address modules.
  • Switch one device to SPI if it supports both protocols.
Common mistake
Assuming a detected address equals device type; always cross-check with the module documentation.

screens.title: SPI basics: MOSI, MISO, SCK, and SS
screens.narratorSegment: SPI is a synchronous serial bus that uses four signals for full-duplex communication: MOSI, which is master out, slave in; MISO, which is master in, slave out; SCK, the serial clock driven by the master; and SS, the slave select line used to enable a specific device. Unlike I2C, each SPI peripheral requires its own SS pin so the master can toggle that device active while leaving others idle. The Arduino Uno provides dedicated MOSI on pin 11, MISO on pin 12, and SCK on pin 13, with a default SS on pin 10; additional devices can use any free digital pin as their SS line. A concrete example is connecting an SD card and a display: both share MOSI/MISO/SCK, but each has a distinct SS pin so the master selects the card when reading files and the display when updating pixels. A frequent misconception is that SPI is always complicated to wire; in fact it is simple and fast but needs more pins than I2C. The takeaway: choose SPI when you need higher throughput and can spare pins for extra SS lines.

keyIdea.title: SPI definition
keyIdea.text: SPI uses MOSI, MISO, SCK, plus one SS per device; it favors speed and simplicity at the cost of extra select lines.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › SPI basics
Signal names
MOSI: master transmits to slaves. MISO: slaves send data to master. SCK: clock from master. SS: individual select lines for each slave.
Arduino Uno pins
MOSI = D11, MISO = D12, SCK = D13, default SS = D10. Use other pins for additional SS lines as needed.
Example scenario
An SD card and an SPI display share MOSI/MISO/SCK. The master pulls the SD card's SS low to read files, then raises it before selecting the display with its SS line. Proper SS handling prevents bus contention.
Misconception
Sharing SS lines will cause devices to respond at the same time unless each device has its own dedicated SS pin toggled correctly.

screens.title: SPI wiring and master/slave behavior
screens.narratorSegment: The SPI architecture is straightforward: the master drives the clock and initiates transfers, and each slave remains passive until its slave select line is asserted. All devices listen to the same MOSI and SCK lines; slaves drive MISO only when they are selected so the master can read their responses without collisions. Practically, you wire MOSI, MISO, and SCK in parallel to all devices, and run a separate SS line from the master to each peripheral. On Arduino Uno the hardware SPI pins are fixed, so using hardware SPI improves performance. A concrete wiring example shows an SD card with SS on pin 4 and an SPI display with SS on pin 7; the master toggles pin 4 low to talk to the card, then drives it high and pulls pin 7 low to update the display. A common pitfall is forgetting to deselect a slave before selecting another, which can create bus contention and corrupted data. The architectural takeaway is that SPI's simplicity yields high speed, but correct selection logic is essential for reliable multi-device operation. SPI wiring and master/slave behavior means the master controls clock and selects devices; slaves only drive the miso line when selected to prevent bus conflicts.. In practical terms, how multiple devices share data lines and use ss for selection. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Master-driven bus
keyIdea.text: The master controls clock and selects devices; slaves only drive the MISO line when selected to prevent bus conflicts.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › SPI Architecture
Shared lines and selects
MOSI, MISO, and SCK are common to all devices. Each device gets a dedicated SS pin to be driven low when selected. The master must toggle SS lines correctly to avoid collisions.
SD card: SS = D4
Display: SS = D7
Master: drives SCK and toggles SS
Common mistake
Leaving a device selected when starting a new transfer often causes bus contention. Always deassert previous SS lines before asserting another.
Key takeaway
Proper SS sequencing is as important as wiring MOSI/MISO/SCK correctly for multi-device SPI systems.

screens.title: Using the SPI library and SPI.transfer()
screens.narratorSegment: Arduino's SPI library simplifies byte-level transfers across the bus. The typical flow is to begin SPI, configure clock speed and data mode if necessary, pull the desired slave select line low, call a transfer function to send a byte and receive a response, and then release the SS line. The function commonly used, transfer, both writes and reads a byte in a single operation. A concrete example is reading a status byte from an SPI peripheral: assert the device's SS, call transfer with a command byte, then call transfer again to clock out the returned data. Remember to match the device's expected clock polarity and phase, otherwise data shifts will misalign and you will see garbage. A common misconception is that SPI. transfer only sends bytes; it actually performs full-duplex transfers so you can read a response simultaneously. The practical takeaway is to manage SS lines manually, set the correct SPI settings for each device, and use the library to abstract the low-level clock toggling while you focus on framing and commands. Using the SPI library and SPI.transfer() means initialize spi, set speed/mode, toggle ss low, use spi.transfer to exchange bytes, then release ss to finish the transaction.. In practical terms, sending and receiving data with arduino's spi api. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › SPI.transfer()
Typical pattern
  1. Call SPI.begin() and set SPI settings for speed and mode.
  2. Pull the device's SS line LOW to select it.

screens.title: I2C vs SPI: feature table and trade-offs
screens.narratorSegment: Choosing between I2C and SPI requires weighing a few consistent trade-offs. I2C uses two lines and a 7-bit address per device, making it ideal when pin economy is critical. It tends to be slower and uses open-drain signaling with pull-ups. SPI needs four lines plus one select per device; it is faster and operates in full duplex, which suits high-throughput peripherals like SD cards and displays. Many devices support both interfaces; in those cases look at the rest of your project: if you already have many I2C parts, adding another sensor is easy. If you need speed for streaming data or the peripheral does not support I2C, SPI is the better choice. A practical example: three low-speed sensors and a small OLED — prefer I2C to conserve pins. Conversely, a camera module or SD card streamer typically needs SPI for speed. A common misconception is that one protocol is always superior; instead, pick the one that fits your constraints and device support. The takeaway: use I2C for pin-limited, multi-device setups and SPI for speed and device-level simplicity. screens.title: Common mistakes and debugging tips
screens.narratorSegment: Real projects often run into a few recurring issues when using I2C and SPI. For I2C, the first mistake is missing or duplicate pull-ups. Some breakout boards provide pull-ups and others do not; measure or check documentation. Without proper pull-ups, signals never reach a valid high state and devices fail to respond. Next, address conflicts occur when two devices share the same default 7-bit address. Running an I2C scanner immediately reveals this and lets you decide to change the module's address, add a multiplexer, or use SPI for one device. For SPI, a common issue is incorrect SS handling: if multiple devices are left selected, their outputs can drive the MISO line simultaneously causing corrupted reads. Always deassert previous selects before asserting the next one. Also confirm SPI clock polarity and phase settings for each device; mismatched modes lead to shifted bits and nonsense data. A quick debugging routine is: verify power rails, run a scanner for I2C, check SS sequencing for SPI, and test with a single device before adding more. The takeaway is that methodical checks save time over guessing at faults.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we explore two essential communication buses used with Arduino: I2C and SPI. You will learn what makes I2C efficient for sharing two wires across many devices using addresses, and why SPI is chosen when you need higher speed and lower latency. We will walk through Arduino pin assignments for both buses, look at common devices that use each protocol, and practice reading and writing with library examples. You will also see how to detect address conflicts on an I2C bus and how to wire multiple SPI devices using separate select lines. These skills matter because they let you expand a single microcontroller into a larger system of sensors, displays, and storage without running out of pins. By the end you will be able to pick the right bus, wire it reliably, and use simple Arduino code to communicate with peripherals. As you explore, notice trade-offs: pin count, speed, and device support. Think about a small project you might build and which protocol would fit it best.

These four objectives map to the practical skills you need for working with I2C and SPI. First, you'll explain the technical differences between the two buses and what each signal means. Understanding that difference helps you choose the right interface for a sensor or display. Second, you'll wire multiple I2C devices to the same bus and manage unique 7-bit addresses; we will practice finding addresses and resolving conflicts. Third, you'll identify the SPI signal names—MOSI, MISO, SCK, and SS—and wire multiple SPI devices, including how to use separate slave select lines. Finally, you'll make protocol choices for common parts by weighing pin count, speed, and library support. Each objective includes hands-on practice so you learn to reason about trade-offs instead of memorizing facts. By the end you should be able to explain your choice to a peer and sketch the wiring for a small multi-device project with confidence.

This second objectives screen focuses on applying the theory. You will practice wiring an I2C LCD and an I2C real-time clock to the same bus and display the current time on the LCD using library objects. You will also run an I2C scanner to identify device addresses and spot conflicts. For SPI you'll wire an SPI device like an SD card or a display and verify proper slave select handling. The assessment idea asks you to choose a protocol for three sensors and a display when digital pins are limited; your correct answer should justify choosing I2C because it uses only two wires for multiple devices. These activities cement the connection between concept and practice, so you are not just naming signals but wiring and coding working systems. Keep an eye out for common mistakes like forgetting pull-up resistors on I2C or sharing SS lines between devices.

I2C is a bus designed to let many devices share the same two wires: one for data and one for the clock. The data line is called SDA and the clock is SCL. Each device on the bus has a 7-bit address used by the master to initiate communication and target a peripheral. This means you can wire multiple sensors and small displays to the same two pins as long as no two devices use the same address. A typical Arduino Uno maps SDA to analog pin A4 and SCL to A5, although newer boards expose dedicated SDA and SCL pins. A concrete example is an I2C LCD and an I2C temperature sensor both connected to SDA and SCL; the master writes a display update to the LCD address and polls the sensor address for readings. A common misconception is that I2C requires no pull-ups: in fact both SDA and SCL are open-drain and need pull-up resistors on the bus to create valid logic highs. The key takeaway is that I2C trades speed for a minimal wiring footprint; use it when pin economy is more important than maximum throughput. How would you check addresses before wiring a second device?

Wiring multiple I2C devices follows a simple process but with a few checks to keep the bus healthy. First, connect all device SDA pins together and all SCL pins together, and connect those two lines to the Arduino SDA and SCL pins — on an Uno that is usually analog A4 and A5. Second, ensure appropriate pull-up resistors are present on SDA and SCL; some breakout boards include them, otherwise add 4.7 kilo-ohm resistors to 5 volts. Third, power each device and run an I2C scanner sketch to list active 7-bit addresses. The scanner identifies addresses so you can check for collisions. Fourth, if two devices share the same address, resolve it by changing the device address if possible, using an address translator, or moving to SPI for one of the parts. A concrete example: if a DS3231 clock and an OLED both show the same default address, run the scanner, then change the OLED's address via its configuration or use a software I2C multiplexer. A common misconception is that devices auto-negotiate addresses; they do not. The key takeaway is to always scan first and verify pull-ups; that prevents hours of debugging.

When programming I2C devices on Arduino, libraries encapsulate the low-level addressing and data framing so you work with objects instead of toggling pins. The Wire library provides the I2C primitives and many device libraries build on it. A common pattern is to create an object with the device address and call methods to send data. For example, a LiquidCrystal I2C library often uses a constructor that takes an address and display dimensions. In code you include the Wire header, include the device library, and instantiate the display object with its hex address and size. Conceptually, this object hides repeated start conditions, address bytes, and byte-level writes so you call familiar methods to print text. A concrete example: creating a display object at address 0x27 for a 16-by-2 LCD lets you call a method to set the cursor and print the time. A trap to avoid is assuming the default address for all modules — always scan to find the actual address. The takeaway is that library objects make code more readable and reduce mistakes, but you must still wire correctly and confirm addresses before relying on default constructors.

An I2C scanner sketch is the first diagnostic you should run on a new bus. It probes all possible 7-bit addresses and reports which ones respond. Running the scanner requires only the Wire library and a simple loop that attempts to begin transmission to each address; a responding device makes the library return success and you print the address. A concrete example output might list addresses like 0x27 and 0x68. Seeing two identical addresses indicates a conflict: two devices claim the same address and will not cooperate. The correct response is to check documentation for address selection options, change hardware configuration jumpers, use a multiplexer device, or move one peripheral to SPI if possible. A common misconception is that the scanner will test advanced features; it only reports that a device responded at that address. Use the scanner as an early check before writing higher-level code. The takeaway is simple: scanning saves time by confirming which devices are visible and where conflicts may exist. In practical terms, detect addresses and resolve conflicts before integrating devices. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

SPI is a synchronous serial bus that uses four signals for full-duplex communication: MOSI, which is master out, slave in; MISO, which is master in, slave out; SCK, the serial clock driven by the master; and SS, the slave select line used to enable a specific device. Unlike I2C, each SPI peripheral requires its own SS pin so the master can toggle that device active while leaving others idle. The Arduino Uno provides dedicated MOSI on pin 11, MISO on pin 12, and SCK on pin 13, with a default SS on pin 10; additional devices can use any free digital pin as their SS line. A concrete example is connecting an SD card and a display: both share MOSI/MISO/SCK, but each has a distinct SS pin so the master selects the card when reading files and the display when updating pixels. A frequent misconception is that SPI is always complicated to wire; in fact it is simple and fast but needs more pins than I2C. The takeaway: choose SPI when you need higher throughput and can spare pins for extra SS lines.

The SPI architecture is straightforward: the master drives the clock and initiates transfers, and each slave remains passive until its slave select line is asserted. All devices listen to the same MOSI and SCK lines; slaves drive MISO only when they are selected so the master can read their responses without collisions. Practically, you wire MOSI, MISO, and SCK in parallel to all devices, and run a separate SS line from the master to each peripheral. On Arduino Uno the hardware SPI pins are fixed, so using hardware SPI improves performance. A concrete wiring example shows an SD card with SS on pin 4 and an SPI display with SS on pin 7; the master toggles pin 4 low to talk to the card, then drives it high and pulls pin 7 low to update the display. A common pitfall is forgetting to deselect a slave before selecting another, which can create bus contention and corrupted data. The architectural takeaway is that SPI's simplicity yields high speed, but correct selection logic is essential for reliable multi-device operation. SPI wiring and master/slave behavior means the master controls clock and selects devices; slaves only drive the miso line when selected to prevent bus conflicts.. Arduino's SPI library simplifies byte-level transfers across the bus. The typical flow is to begin SPI, configure clock speed and data mode if necessary, pull the desired slave select line low, call a transfer function to send a byte and receive a response, and then release the SS line. The function commonly used, transfer, both writes and reads a byte in a single operation. Here are three compact reminders to keep at hand while you build. First, remember Arduino Uno pin mappings: SDA and SCL are on analog pins A4 and A5; SPI hardware pins are D11, D12, and D13 with a default SS on D10. Second, always run an I2C scanner after wiring to list active 7-bit addresses and catch conflicts early. Third, when using SPI, manage SS lines carefully: deassert one device before asserting another and set the correct clock mode for each peripheral.
